description: After Troy, Odysseus, king of Ithaca, takes ten years to get home. Monsters, gods and temptations mark out a voyage that invents the cunning hero of Western literature.

hero.hook: Ten years to get home: the greatest journey back in all of literature.

blocks.text: Around the **8th century BC**, a long Greek poem tells the story of one man coming home. His name is **Odysseus**, king of the small island of **Ithaca**, off the coast of Greece. The Romans called him *Ulysses*. The **Trojan War** ended ten years earlier, a legendary clash between Greeks and Trojans over Queen Helen. His men want to see their homes again. But the voyage takes another **ten years**. This is the **Odyssey**, the second great pillar of European culture alongside the Iliad.

Here the poem no longer sings only the fury of weapons. It follows a hero who survives through **cunning**, the Greek *metis*, through language and through sheer endurance. To get home, Odysseus sometimes has to accept being “**Nobody**.” In Greek that is *Outis*. The password saves his men from the Cyclops. The Odyssey turns the voyage into an inner ordeal, not just an adventure.

The poem is credited to **Homer**, a half-legendary figure about whom almost nothing is known for certain. Was he a single poet, or the name of a long tradition? Modern scholarship, above all [[Milman Parry]], an American philologist of the 20th century, shows that the text grew out of an [[oral tradition]]. For centuries, [[aedes]] composed live. These poet-singers improvised while accompanying themselves on a lyre. They worked from ready-made phrasing, the [[Homeric formula]]: “resourceful Odysseus,” “rosy-fingered Dawn.” Those repeated phrases made memorizing and composing much easier.
In Greek, the name *Homeros* can suggest “the one who does not see.” Hence the legend of a blind poet walking from city to city, carrying the epic in his memory rather than on a scroll.

The epic runs to roughly **12,000 lines** of [[Homeric Greek]] and **24 books**. Homeric Greek is an archaic literary language that nobody ever spoke that way. The meter is the **dactylic hexameter**, a long line of six feet. Its rhythm comes from the [[dactyl]], a metrical unit that imitates a gallop. Once written down, the poem fixed an artificial language that gives the story a sacred, timeless ring. Hence the [[Homeric question]]: one author, or a collective tradition set down late?

sections.title: Homer, or how poems were sung before they were written

blocks.text: The story opens [[in media res]]. The Latin phrase means “in the middle of things.” Odysseus is held back by the nymph **Calypso**, a goddess who takes him in on her island. The famous adventures come later, as flashback. That device is [[analepsis]], a step back in time inside the narrative. The hero tells them to the **Phaeacians**, a welcoming people who escort him to Ithaca. The warrior becomes the teller of his own legend.

blocks.caption: Odysseus facing the Cyclops Polyphemus on an ancient Greek vase

blocks.text: Everything turns after the **Cyclops Polyphemus**, a one-eyed giant and a son of the god Poseidon. To save his men, Odysseus blinds him, then shouts out his real name. **Poseidon**, god of the sea and father of the giant, hunts him across every sea from then on. Among the **Lotus-Eaters**, he drags his companions out of the forgetfulness caused by an intoxicating plant. In the house of **Circe**, a sorceress who turns men into animals, he wins their human shape back. Every stop tests **hospitality**, the *xenia* that was a core value of the ancient Greek world. The [[nekyia]], the descent to the underworld to question the dead, brings him up against his own limit: speaking to shadows, accepting what is lost.

sections.title: The wandering: monsters, forgetting and hospitality

blocks.text: Meanwhile, on Ithaca, Queen **Penelope**, the faithful wife of Odysseus, holds out against the **suitors**. A hundred noblemen are eating their way through the palace while they wait for her to marry one of them. She promises to remarry when the shroud for **Laertes**, her father-in-law, is finished, then unpicks her work every night. This is cunning in a female form, a mirror of the hero's own.

blocks.caption: Penelope weaving by day and unpicking by night to buy time against the suitors

blocks.text: Odysseus is recognized first by his old dog **Argos**, then by his nurse **Eurycleia**, before Penelope tests him with the secret of their bed, carved from a living olive tree. That intimate detail proves he really is the king and not an impostor.

Disguised as a beggar by **Athena**, goddess of wisdom and protector of Odysseus, the hero watches first, then strikes. The archery contest is famous: only Odysseus can string the king's bow. Then come the slaughter of the suitors and the return of order to the palace. The **nostos**, the homecoming, is not only a journey across the map. Home is not a house: it is a bond you prove and an identity you win back.

sections.title: Ithaca: the homecoming and the olive-wood bed

blocks.text: Odysseus is not an invincible demigod like **Achilles**. His weapon is adaptation. He accepts humiliation, lies when he has to, weeps, doubts. In the 20th century, [[James Joyce]] moved that wandering into a single day in Dublin in his novel **Ulysses**, published in 1922. From the poet **Du Bellay** and his “Happy the man who, like Ulysses, made a fine voyage” to the movies, the castaway looking for his homeland is still a story engine. The Odyssey asks a simple question: is immortality without risk worth more than a human life, fragile and chosen?

blocks.text: The **Odyssey** invents the hero who gets home through cunning and endurance. The point of the voyage is not the immortality Calypso offered, but a human life, fragile and chosen, found again on Ithaca.
